mcqs.question: What can an interactive debugger show you that print-statement debugging generally can't, without editing and rerunning code?
options: The exact commit that introduced the bug
Any variable currently in scope, including ones you didn't think to log in advance
Whether the bug is a memory-safety issue
The full history of every value a variable has ever held
mcqs.explanation: Once paused at a breakpoint, a debugger lets you inspect any in-scope variable on the spot, including ones you never anticipated needing — print debugging only shows what you thought to log ahead of time and requires an edit-rerun cycle to add more. Finding the introducing commit is git bisect's job, and full historical values need a record-replay tool, not a plain debugger.

mcqs.question: A bug only manifests on iteration 4,982 of a 50,000-iteration loop. What's the most efficient way to catch it with a debugger?
options: Set a plain breakpoint on the loop body and click continue 4,982 times
Add a manual counter variable and print it every iteration until it reaches 4,982
Set a conditional breakpoint that only stops when the iteration count matches the failing condition
Step through the entire loop from iteration 1 using stepping alone
mcqs.explanation: A conditional breakpoint is evaluated silently on every pass and only interrupts execution when its expression matches, which is exactly what a rare, state-dependent bug needs. Clicking continue thousands of times or stepping through the whole loop wastes enormous time doing manually what the debugger can do for you.

mcqs.question: You know a regression exists somewhere in the last 1,000 commits and have an automated test that reproduces it. What's the fastest way to find the introducing commit?
options: git bisect run with the test command, letting git automatically check out and test each midpoint
Manually check out every commit from oldest to newest and run the test on each
Read the diff of every commit looking for anything that touches the affected code
Check out only the most recent 50 commits, since regressions are usually recent
mcqs.explanation: git bisect run automates the binary search entirely — git checks out each midpoint, runs the test, reads the exit code, and continues, resolving a 1,000-commit range in about 10 steps with zero manual judgment calls. Checking every commit or reading every diff scales with the range size instead of its logarithm, and assuming recency can simply be wrong.

mcqs.question: A corrupted value is discovered at line 400, but it was actually written incorrectly at line 40, twenty calls earlier. Why is this the case where record-replay debugging most earns its overhead?
options: It lets you edit the historical execution to test a fix without rerunning
It automatically identifies which commit introduced the corruption
It records execution once and lets you step backward or query "last write to this value" instead of re-running with creeping breakpoints
It removes the need to reproduce the bug at all
mcqs.explanation: Record-replay lets you record the execution once and then move backward through it, including jumping straight to the last write of a value, which turns a multi-hour hunt with re-run after re-run into a single query. It doesn't identify commits (that's bisect) or let you edit history, and you still need a working repro to record in the first place.

mcqs.question: Why do memory-safety sanitizers (AddressSanitizer, etc.) matter for bugs like use-after-free, when the program would eventually crash anyway?
options: They catch the mistake at the exact moment it occurs, instead of at whatever later, unrelated point the corruption happens to crash the program
They replace the need for a debugger entirely in native-code development
They fix the memory bug automatically once detected
They only work in production environments, not in CI
mcqs.explanation: Memory corruption often doesn't crash where the mistake happens — it silently corrupts state and crashes somewhere unrelated, much later, making the real cause hard to trace. A sanitizer instruments the binary to flag the violation at the actual moment it occurs, turning a baffling later crash into a precise stack trace. They don't fix bugs automatically and their overhead makes them a CI/testing tool, not a production one.

mcqs.question: What's the most reliable way to prevent debug-only code (bypassed auth checks, debug endpoints, verbose logging) from reaching production?
options: Trust engineers to remove debug code before committing
A process-level safeguard — PR checklist items and linter rules that flag known debug patterns — rather than relying purely on individual discipline
Only allow debugging in a separate branch that's never merged
Disable all debug tooling in the IDE so it can't be used at all
mcqs.explanation: Relying on memory or discipline alone is exactly how debug endpoints and bypassed auth checks ship — the fix that actually holds is a structural one: checklist items and linter rules that catch known patterns like console.log or set_trace calls before merge. Disabling debug tooling entirely would cripple legitimate debugging, and a never-merged branch doesn't stop debug code written directly on a feature branch.
